sections.b: 2 Peter is written as the apostle's farewell: grow in the virtues that make your calling firm (1:3–11), remember the apostles' eyewitness testimony and the prophets (1:12–21), beware of false teachers (chapter 2, reworking Jude), and do not believe the mockers who say Christ will not come (chapter 3). It is the most doubted book of the New Testament and the main text for the teaching that believers share in God's nature (1:4).

2 Peter keeps Jude's argument but reshapes it. It turns Jude's report (intruders "slipped in among you without being noticed," Jude 4) into a prediction that is already coming true (2 Peter 2:1, 10). It names no book outside Scripture: no quotation of 1 Enoch (Jude 14–15) and no Michael disputing with the devil (Jude 9), only "angels" (2 Peter 2:11). It reorders the examples to follow Genesis (angels, flood, Sodom) and adds two people God rescued, Noah and Lot (2 Peter 2:5–9). It drops Cain and Korah, shortens Jude's four pictures from nature to two (2 Peter 2:17), and gives the mockers of Jude 18 their own words: "Where is the promise of his coming?" (2 Peter 3:4). Several of Jude's words reappear in near-twins: "sunken rocks" (spilades) becomes "stains" (spiloi), and "love feasts" (agapais) becomes "deceptions" (apatais), though some copies of 2 Peter have "love feasts" there too.

sections.h: Translating the two letters side by side
sections.b: On this site the two letters are translated the same way where the Greek is the same and differently exactly where it differs, so a reader can compare them. For example, both say the teachers "slander the glorious ones" (Jude 8; 2 Peter 2:10) and that angels do not "bring a slanderous judgment" (Jude 9; 2 Peter 2:11); both call the teachers "animals that cannot think" (Jude 10; 2 Peter 2:12) and say they "feast with you" (Jude 12; 2 Peter 2:13); and darkness "has been kept" for them (Jude 13; 2 Peter 2:17). Where Jude has "waterless clouds" 2 Peter has "waterless springs," and where Jude says "In the last time there will be mockers," 2 Peter says "in the last days mockers will come with their mocking."

common: 2 Peter used Jude and left out its quotations from books outside Scripture.
uncommon: Jude came second: Luther wrote that Jude took nearly all its words from 2 Peter.

sections.b: 2 Peter presents itself as Peter's last word before his death, which Jesus had shown him (2 Peter 1:14; compare John 21:18–19). It opens with his Hebrew name, "Simeon Peter" (as in Acts 15:14), recalls the voice he heard on the holy mountain (2 Peter 1:16–18), and calls Paul "our beloved brother" (2 Peter 3:15), a striking word after their clash at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14). Most critical scholars think a follower wrote it in Peter's name after his death; a minority defend Peter as the author. See the topic page The Second Letter of Peter.

sections.b: 2 Peter 1:4 is the key text: through God's promises believers "become sharers in the divine nature," having escaped the world's decay. Orthodox theology builds on it (Athanasius: "He was made man that we might be made God"; Vladimir Lossky: "in deification we are by grace ... all that God is by nature"); the Catholic Catechism cites the verse (460); Calvin read "nature" as "quality," not essence, yet spoke of God's aim "to deify us"; Wesley read it as renewal in God's image and communion with him; and the Finnish school of Luther research finds the idea in Luther, while the Formula of Concord rejects a righteousness of faith that is God's own essential righteousness dwelling in us. The verse itself joins the gift to effort: the next verses ask for a life of goodness, self-control and love (2 Peter 1:5–7).

2 Peter 1:16–18 is the only place outside the Gospels that tells of the transfiguration. The writer claims to have been there "on the holy mountain" and heard the voice: "My Son, my dearly loved one, is this. In him I have found delight" (2 Peter 1:17), in words that differ from all three Gospels (Matthew 17:5; Mark 9:7; Luke 9:35). The scene is offered as proof that the apostles' message about Christ's "power and coming" was no myth: the glory they saw was a preview of the glory to come.

2 Peter 1:20–21 says that no prophecy of Scripture came "by human will"; instead, "people borne along by the Holy Spirit spoke from God." The verb is used of a ship driven by the wind. With 2 Timothy 3:16 it is the main biblical text on inspiration. It affirms that the source is God and that the speakers were human; how the two worked together it does not explain. Wesley thought the prophets "were purely passive"; most later theologians stress that God used the writers' own minds and styles.

Two verses in 2 Peter enter this debate. 2 Peter 1:20 says no prophecy of Scripture comes "by a person's own interpretation": either the prophet did not invent his message, or readers may not explain it as they please. 2 Peter 3:16 warns that "ignorant and unsteady people" twist Paul's letters "as they also twist the other Scriptures." Catholic teaching cites these verses (Dei Verbum 11) and entrusts authentic interpretation to the Church's teaching office (Dei Verbum 10); the Westminster Confession makes "the Scripture itself" the rule of interpretation (1.9). See the card on 2 Peter 1.

2 Peter had the hardest road of any New Testament book. Its earliest manuscript is Papyrus 72 (third or fourth century). Origen called a second letter of Peter "doubtful"; Eusebius said it "does not belong to the canon" but was used with the other Scriptures, and listed it among the disputed books; Jerome said many denied it to Peter because of its style. Athanasius included "of Peter, two" in his list of AD 367, and the churches have received it ever since. 2 Peter 3:16 is also the only place where a New Testament letter explicitly sets Paul's letters beside "the other Scriptures" (compare 1 Timothy 5:18, which may call a saying of Jesus "Scripture").

2 Peter 2:4 retells Jude 6 with a Greek word: God "threw them into Tartarus," the deepest prison of the underworld in Greek myth, where Hesiod has Zeus bind the Titans. Jewish writers used the word too: 1 Enoch 20:2 sets the archangel Uriel "over the world and over Tartarus." Unlike Jude, 2 Peter gives no detail of the angels' sin and does not quote 1 Enoch. Manuscripts differ on whether they are held in "chains" (as Jude 6) or "pits" of gloom.

2 Peter 2:5 calls Noah "the eighth one" (Noah and seven others, as 1 Peter 3:20 counts) and "a herald of righteousness." Genesis does not say Noah preached, but Jewish tradition did: Josephus says he urged the people to change their ways, and the Sibylline Oracles give him a sermon calling for repentance. In 2 Peter he is a model for believers who announce a coming judgment to a world that mocks it (2 Peter 3:3–6).

sections.h: The flood as proof against the mockers
sections.b: 2 Peter uses the flood twice: as an example of God's judgment and rescue (2 Peter 2:5), and as the answer to mockers who say everything has gone on unchanged since creation (2 Peter 3:4–6). The world "that took shape out of water" was "flooded with water and came to ruin," and the present heavens and earth are kept, by the same word, for fire on the day of judgment (2 Peter 3:7).

2 Peter 2:6 says God "reduced the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes" and set them up as an example. Unlike Jude 7, it does not repeat the charge of going "after other flesh," but it adds the rescue of Lot (2 Peter 2:7–8), who was worn down by the lawless way of life around him.

2 Peter 2:7–8 calls Lot "righteous" three times and describes him as tormented day after day by what he saw and heard in Sodom. Genesis 19 shows a more mixed man, rescued "because the LORD had pity on him" (Genesis 19:16). 2 Peter follows Jewish tradition, as in Wisdom 10:6, where Wisdom rescues "the righteous man" from the fire on the five cities. The point is that God knows how to rescue the godly (2 Peter 2:9).

sections.h: Balaam son of Bosor, and the donkey
sections.b: 2 Peter 2:15–16 makes Balaam the model of the greedy teacher, "who loved the pay for wrongdoing," and recalls the story of Numbers 22:21–35: "a voiceless beast of burden, speaking out in a human voice, stopped the prophet's madness" (2 Peter 2:16). Most Greek editions call him "son of Bosor" rather than the "son of Beor" of Numbers 22:5 (Westcott and Hort printed Beor, Thayer's lexicon notes); explanations include a way of pronouncing the Hebrew name and a pun on Hebrew basar, "flesh."

sections.h: "Where is the promise of his coming?"
sections.b: 2 Peter quotes and answers a mocking denial of Christ's return: "Where is the promise of his coming?" (2 Peter 3:4). The apostles saw his glory on the mountain (2 Peter 1:16–18); God has judged the world before (2 Peter 3:5–7); his time is not ours (2 Peter 3:8); the delay is patience (2 Peter 3:9); and the day will come like a thief (2 Peter 3:10). Believers wait for it and can "hurry it along" by holy lives (2 Peter 3:11–12).

sections.h: A thousand years like one day
sections.b: 2 Peter 3:8–9 is the New Testament's most direct answer to the delay of Christ's coming. Using Psalm 90:4, it says that "in the Lord's sight one day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day," and it explains the delay as patience: God "does not want any to be lost, but wants all to arrive at repentance." Jubilees used Psalm 90:4 to measure time, and early Christians such as the writer of Barnabas and Irenaeus used it to count six thousand years of history; 2 Peter does no counting.

2 Peter 3:10–12 joins two pictures of the day of the Lord: it comes "like a thief" (as 1 Thessalonians 5:2), and it brings fire, as the prophets said (Isaiah 66:15–16; Malachi 4:1). The heavens go by with a rushing roar, the elements burn and are dissolved, and the earth and its works "will lie exposed" (in Greek "will be found," a much-debated reading). 2 Peter also calls it "God's day" (2 Peter 3:12) and "the day of judgment" (2 Peter 3:7).

2 Peter 3:13 promises "new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness makes its home" (Isaiah 65:17; Isaiah 66:22). Whether the old world is annihilated first depends partly on the manuscripts of 2 Peter 3:10: the KJV's "shall be burned up" suggests destruction, while the oldest Greek, "will be found" (the Plain: "will lie exposed"), has been read as exposure for judgment or, by Al Wolters, as refining, after which the same creation comes out purified. The flood, which ended "the world of that day" without abolishing the earth (2 Peter 3:6), is the letter's model.

2 Peter uses stoicheia without "of the world": the elements "will burn and be dissolved" (2 Peter 3:10) and "burn and melt" (2 Peter 3:12). Readings: the physical elements of the world (where Thayer's lexicon places these verses), the heavenly bodies (sun, moon and stars, a sense of stoicheia in early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr), or the spirit powers thought to rule them. Because the list runs heavens, elements, earth, the heavenly bodies fit well, as in Isaiah 34:4. This is a different use from Paul's "basic elements of the world" (Galatians 4:3).

2 Peter 3:3 repeats the apostles' warning (Jude 18) that "in the last days mockers will come," and gives their words: "Where is the promise of his coming?" The letter treats the mockers as a sign that the last days have come, not as evidence against them.

2 Peter 3:15–16 calls Paul "our beloved brother," agrees with what he wrote about God's patience, admits that his letters contain "some things hard to grasp," and warns that some twist them "as they also twist the other Scriptures." It is the only New Testament passage that sets Paul's letters, apparently as a collection, beside Scripture.

sections.h: Worse off at the end (2 Peter 2:20–22)
sections.b: 2 Peter 2:20–22 speaks of people who "escaped the filth of the world by knowing the Lord and Savior" and were tangled in it again, so that "in the end they are worse off than at the beginning"; it would have been better never to have known the way. Wesley read it as a real fall, of people "after they have made shipwreck of the faith"; Calvin held that the faithful, though they sin, "do not fall away from the grace of God," and read it of people whose change, like the washed sow's, never reached their nature. The card at Hebrews 6:4–6 sets out the churches' answers.

2 Peter 2 predicts false teachers as Israel had false prophets: they sneak in factions, disown the Master who bought them, and exploit the church for money (2 Peter 2:1–3). Their lives give them away: greed, sexual looseness, contempt for authority, empty promises of freedom (2 Peter 2:10–19). Chapter 3 shows their teaching: no coming, no judgment (2 Peter 3:3–4).

2 Peter takes the form of a farewell testament, like Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49), Moses' last speeches, Paul's farewell at Miletus (Acts 20:17–38) and Jesus' words at the Last Supper: the speaker's death is near (2 Peter 1:14), he wants to be remembered (2 Peter 1:15), and he foretells trouble after his departure (2 Peter 2:1–3; 2 Peter 3:3).

sections.h: A lamp until the day dawns
sections.b: 2 Peter 1:19 calls the prophetic word "a lamp that shines in a murky place, until day shines through and the morning star comes up in your hearts," and 1:21 says prophecy came not by human will but from people "borne along by the Holy Spirit." The prophets and the apostles are set side by side (2 Peter 3:2).
